### Three ways the judge can get the answer wrong

1. **The arms influence which behaviors earn credit.** Ratchet supplied 42 `Open:` lines and 37 after-build additions. Even if both raters approve an item on its merits, the combined inventory can overrepresent situations Ratchet already considered. Freeze the primary inventory from the request, starting files, and independent listers before the merger or raters see arm findings. For each distinct obligation, record who cares, when it applies, which outcomes are acceptable, and what failure costs. Use arm-derived items as a sensitivity check. A win that depends on them needs independent confirmation.
2. **The auditors can give each product a different exam.** Cross-probing corrects uneven discovery only for defects someone finds. Section 9’s four ticket probes found two shared gaps and two behaviors ShipLoop already handled. Run the same scenarios with the same fixtures, limits, and pass criteria on all three products, adapting commands to each interface. Record missing observations explicitly. Lock runtime grades before showing auditors the specs and authored tests. Independently rerun observations that could decide the result, including apparent passes.
3. **A single serious failure can disappear in the tally.** Suppose ShipLoop alone loses a confirmed write during supported use. That can fall below both two-item margins, so even unanimous preference for Ratchet leaves ShipLoop “nearly competitive.” Set severity gates and a concrete tolerance before auditing. For example, require verified coverage, zero additional missed mandatory behaviors or high-severity failures, and at most one additional low-impact shortfall. If missing evidence or judge disagreement could change that result, call it inconclusive. If repairability matters, run a capped Sol-medium follow-up on a decision-relevant case, rerun the common probes, and compare the repaired product’s quality and all-in cost with Ratchet’s. An hour is roughly two to six ShipLoop deliveries.

### Where size can buy points

| Reading | Control |
|---|---|
| **D1** | A fixed, deduplicated inventory of stated obligations already limits padding. Count each obligation once and keep its importance independent of how many clauses describe it. |
| **D2** | Count one credit per preselected obligation. Require the named test to pass on the delivery and fail for the expected reason when the observable behavior breaks. Duplicate assertions and tests of internals can make a suite look thorough while leaving the same regression undetected. |
| **D3** | Use the same independent inventory and denominator for every product. Collapse variants of the same obligation. Credit any acceptable outcome, including a sensible default the arm never wrote down. |
| **D4** | Fix the denominator to decisions a requester or maintainer needs to know, including decisions the product leaves unhandled. Give one credit for an accurate, findable account of what ships in the material the requester receives. An `Open:` marker alone earns zero. |
| **D5** | Longer artifacts can direct or bury an auditor’s attention. Give each product the same discovery budget and cross-probe the same failure scenarios. Collapse multiple reproductions of one defect and anchor severity to harm under supported use. |
| **D6** | An audit can betray which product had the longer spec and repeat evidence already scored in D1–D5. Give judges uniform evidence per item, remove volume and provenance cues, and counterbalance order. Use their judgment to resolve materiality and disputed evidence. Count each consequence once. |

With one run per arm per case, the verdict applies to these deliveries. Attributing any advantage specifically to specification length requires varying length while holding the rest of the workflow fixed.

### Calibration and one cut

**The current check is too weak.** An auditor that reliably catches only 13 of 27 mutants passes the two-of-three detection bar on 47% of uniform draws. The clean reference can receive false `partly` ratings or invented defect reports and still pass. The check also leaves the final decision rule untested.

Use the same four audit slots for a blinded end-to-end check. Take the clean reference, a copy with padded prose and redundant assertions, one consequential existing mutant of a stated behavior, and one independently verified failure of an unstated obligation. Freeze the answer key first. Require the clean and padded versions to tie without false deficits, both planted faults to reproduce at the expected severity, and a single material fault to change the verdict. Counterbalance presentation order. If the instrument changes, rerun on fresh held-back controls and record both attempts.

**Cut the exhaustive D2 census.** Verify test strength on a small, shared set of high-risk obligations. Mutating and rerunning tests for every stated item across twelve products would spend most of that effort on coverage differences unlikely to change the decision.
